Feng"}, {"authorId": "2314465043", "name": "Xinping Ren"}, {"authorId": "50557831", "name": "Chang-Zhu Liu"}, {"authorId": "2178454434", "name": "Tao Song"}, {"authorId": "46413121", "name": "Fan-Kun Meng"}, {"authorId": "2144531803", "name": "Yao Zhang"}, {"authorId": "2405393346", "name": "Ye Fang"}, {"authorId": "148086586", "name": "Su-Mei Ma"}, {"authorId": "2317905602", "name": "Jinfeng Wang"}, {"authorId": "2376149395", "name": "Jie Tian"}, {"authorId": "2241946892", "name": "Xin Yang"}, {"authorId": "2275960658", "name": "Jie Ren"}, {"authorId": "2227945645", "name": "Ping Liang"}, {"authorId": "2119043734", "name": "Kunyang Wang"}], "abstract": "Domain generalization remains a critical challenge in medical ultrasound imaging, where models must maintain robust performance across diverse clinical centers with varying acquisition protocols, equipment vendors, and patient populations. Existing style-based augmentation methods primarily focus on training-time perturbations while neglecting the fundamental train-test distribution mismatch, leading to suboptimal generalization when deployed in unseen medical centers. We propose Multi-Center Adaptive Cross-Domain Style Alignment (MACS), a novel framework that bridges this gap through test-time adaptive normalization guided by domain-specific style prototypes. MACS introduces three key innovations: (1) per-domain covariance modeling that explicitly captures the heterogeneous correlation structures across source medical centers, (2) a lightweight style-based domain classifier that efficiently identifies domain similarity without requiring raw pixel processing, and (3) a soft assignment mechanism that constructs customized normalization targets by weighting multiple source prototypes according to their relevance to each test sample. We validate MACS on a rigorously curated international elastographic ultrasound dataset comprising 1,937 patients with chronic liver disease collected from 17 clinical centers across China, Japan, and Europe. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MACS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art domain generalization methods across multiple cross-domain evaluation settings, achieving superior accuracy and stability. Moreover, ablation studies confirm that the proposed components contribute synergistically to the overall performance. MACS is a plug-and-play solution with negligible computational overhead, enabling real-time inference and making it well suited for practical deployment in multi-center clinical diagnostic scenarios."}}]}
